item.content:encoded:
Young and emerging entrepreneurs with innovative ideas for the cashew sector now have an opportunity to transform their concepts into investment-ready and climate-smart businesses through the e-MOVE Call for Proposals: Build Your AgriCanvas. Build Your Future.

The initiative is designed to support promising agripreneurs who are developing innovative solutions across the cashew value chain. Through a combination of free online learning, business development tools and potential kickstart prizes, participants can strengthen their entrepreneurial ideas and position themselves for future investment and growth.

Submission Window 3 is open from September to October 2026, giving eligible entrepreneurs the opportunity to develop and submit a viable business concept using the AgriCanvas framework.

Successful participants may receive valuable support, including EUR 2,000 in direct funding or business-enabling tools such as a laptop, tablet or software to support their operations.

The application deadline is 30 October 2026.

What Is the e-MOVE Call for Proposals?

The e-MOVE initiative encourages young and emerging entrepreneurs in the agricultural sector to convert knowledge gained through online learning into practical, investment-ready business ideas.

Participants are expected to build on the knowledge and tools acquired through free e-learning courses offered on the e-MOVE platform. The programme focuses on helping entrepreneurs understand important areas of modern agribusiness, including sustainable agricultural practices, investment readiness, business planning and climate resilience.

The Call for Proposals specifically invites innovative ideas connected to the cashew value chain.

Rather than simply submitting a general business idea, applicants are required to demonstrate how their proposed venture can operate as a viable enterprise. This includes developing a clear business model, identifying potential revenue streams, considering climate-smart practices and estimating the capital required to establish or expand the business.

The initiative aims to help promising entrepreneurs move from ideas to actionable business concepts that can potentially attract investment and contribute to sustainable agricultural development.

Why the Cashew Value Chain Matters

Cashew is an important agricultural commodity with significant economic potential across many countries, particularly in Africa and other OACPS member states.

However, the potential of the cashew sector extends beyond primary production. The wider value chain offers opportunities in areas such as:

  • Cashew farming and production
  • Sustainable agricultural practices
  • Processing and value addition
  • Cashew nut processing
  • Packaging
  • Storage and logistics
  • Marketing and distribution
  • Agricultural technology
  • Climate-smart production systems
  • Waste management and by-product utilization
  • Agribusiness services
  • Financial and investment solutions
  • Digital platforms supporting farmers and businesses

Through this Call for Proposals, entrepreneurs are encouraged to think creatively about challenges and opportunities within the cashew ecosystem.

Applicants can develop ideas that improve productivity, increase value addition, strengthen resilience, create employment or introduce innovative business solutions within the sector.

What Are the Benefits of the e-MOVE Call for Proposals?

The programme provides more than just an opportunity to compete for financial support. Participants also gain access to learning resources and business development tools designed to strengthen their entrepreneurial capacity.

1. Opportunity to Receive EUR 2,000 in Direct Funding

Selected winners may receive EUR 2,000 in direct funding to support the development or growth of their business.

The funding can provide an important starting point for entrepreneurs seeking to test, launch, strengthen or scale a promising agribusiness concept.

For early-stage entrepreneurs, access to initial capital can be a major challenge. This opportunity provides selected participants with the possibility of receiving financial support to move their business idea closer to implementation.

2. Opportunity to Receive Business Equipment or Software

Winners may alternatively receive valuable tools to support their business operations, including:

  • A laptop
  • A tablet
  • Software

Digital tools are increasingly important for modern businesses. Equipment and software can help entrepreneurs manage operations, maintain records, communicate with customers, develop marketing strategies and improve overall business efficiency.

3. Free Access to Cashew Sector Learning

Applicants gain access to free e-learning courses designed to strengthen their understanding of agriculture and agribusiness.

The learning pathway helps participants build the knowledge necessary to develop stronger and more practical business ideas.

The courses are offered at no cost, meaning participants do not need to pay tuition or registration fees to access the required learning materials.

4. Development of an Investment-Ready Business Idea

One of the most important aspects of the programme is its focus on investment readiness.

Many entrepreneurs have innovative ideas but struggle to communicate them clearly to investors, partners or financial institutions.

The AgriCanvas process helps applicants structure their ideas by considering key elements of a viable business model.

Participants are encouraged to think about areas such as:

  • The problem their business intends to solve
  • Their target market
  • The products or services they will offer
  • Revenue generation
  • Required resources
  • Climate resilience
  • Business operations
  • Capital requirements
  • Growth potential

This approach can help transform a general business concept into a more structured and fundable proposal.

5. Focus on Climate-Smart and Resilient Agriculture

The initiative places significant emphasis on climate-smart and low-emission agricultural practices.

Applicants are expected to consider how their projects can contribute to environmental sustainability and resilience.

For example, an entrepreneur may consider:

  • Sustainable farming practices
  • Resource-efficient production
  • Climate adaptation strategies
  • Reduced emissions
  • Improved soil conservation
  • Reduced agricultural waste
  • Renewable energy solutions
  • Circular economy approaches
  • Resilient agricultural supply chains

By integrating climate-smart approaches into their business models, entrepreneurs can develop ventures that are better positioned to respond to environmental challenges.

6. Opportunity to Contribute to Sustainable Food Systems

The programme aims to support agricultural enterprises that can contribute to stronger and more sustainable food systems.

Innovative agribusinesses have the potential to:

  • Create employment opportunities
  • Support farmers
  • Increase agricultural productivity
  • Strengthen local economies
  • Improve value addition
  • Reduce post-harvest losses
  • Promote sustainable production
  • Support rural development

By supporting viable MSMEs, the initiative seeks to strengthen the role of young entrepreneurs in building resilient agricultural economies.

Who Can Apply for the e-MOVE Call for Proposals?

The Call for Proposals is designed for young and emerging entrepreneurs with innovative ideas related to the cashew sector.

To qualify, applicants must meet the following requirements.

Applicants Must Be 18 Years or Older

Participants must be at least 18 years old at the time of application.

Applicants Must Be Based in an OACPS Member State

The opportunity is open to individuals based in member states of the Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States (OACPS).

The OACPS represents countries across Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Applicants should confirm whether their country is an eligible OACPS member state before beginning their application.

Applicants Must Have an Innovative Cashew Value Chain Idea

The proposed business concept must focus on one or more aspects of the cashew value chain.

Applicants are encouraged to identify opportunities where innovation can improve existing systems, address challenges or create new economic opportunities.

Applicants Must Complete the Required e-MOVE Training

Completion of the mandatory e-learning pathway is an essential requirement.

Applicants cannot simply submit an idea without completing the required courses.

A valid certificate ID from the final required course must be included in the submission.

How to Apply for the e-MOVE Call for Proposals 2026

Applicants must follow a specific process to ensure that their submission is considered valid.

The application process involves registration, completion of mandatory courses, development of an AgriCanvas and submission of the final business idea.

Step 1: Register on atingi or Access the e-MOVE Landing Page

The first step is to access the e-MOVE learning platform through atingi.

Applicants can access the dedicated e-MOVE landing page, where the required learning resources are grouped together.

The platform provides free courses designed to help participants develop the knowledge necessary to create a stronger agribusiness proposal.

Applicants should ensure they create or use an account that allows them to complete the full learning pathway and access their course certificates.

Step 2: Complete the Mandatory e-MOVE Courses

Applicants must complete the required courses in the specified order.

The learning pathway includes two important stages.

Course 1: Introduction to Conservation Agriculture

The first requirement is to complete the course:

Introduction to Conservation Agriculture (CA)

This course introduces participants to concepts related to sustainable and conservation-focused agricultural practices.

Completing this first stage is necessary before progressing to the next required course.

Course 2: Creating an Investment-Ready Agribusiness

After successfully completing the first course, participants unlock the next required course:

Creating an Investment-Ready Agribusiness

This course is particularly important because it prepares applicants to structure their business ideas and develop proposals that demonstrate investment potential.

Applicants must complete this course successfully and obtain a valid certificate ID.

The certificate ID serves as proof that the applicant has completed the required training pathway.

Step 3: Develop Your AgriCanvas

After completing the required learning, participants must develop their business concept using the Business Model Canvas template provided in the submission module of the Creating an Investment-Ready Agribusiness course.

The AgriCanvas should clearly explain the proposed business idea.

Applicants should use this stage to carefully consider the major components of their proposed venture.

A strong AgriCanvas should demonstrate:

  • A clear business concept
  • A relevant problem or opportunity
  • The proposed solution
  • Target customers or beneficiaries
  • Revenue generation potential
  • Key business activities
  • Required resources
  • Partnerships
  • Operational considerations
  • Financial requirements
  • Climate-smart features
  • Potential for sustainability and growth

Applicants should avoid rushing this stage. A well-developed business model can significantly improve the clarity and strength of a proposal.

Step 4: Submit Your Business Idea Through the Official Form

Once the AgriCanvas is complete, applicants must submit their proposal through the official submission form.

To ensure that a submission is valid, applicants must:

  • Use the certificate ID from the Creating an Investment-Ready Agribusiness course
  • Complete the official submission form
  • Enter the complete AgriCanvas directly into the form
  • Provide all required information
  • Submit through the designated application platform

Applicants should note that file uploads for the AgriCanvas are not accepted.

The full AgriCanvas must be entered directly into the official form.

Only submissions completed through the designated form will be reviewed.

Additional Information Required in the Submission Form

In addition to the AgriCanvas, applicants will be asked to provide short written information about important aspects of their project.

These additional questions are designed to help evaluators understand the practicality and sustainability of the proposed business idea.

Describe the Climate-Smart or Resilience Component

Applicants must explain how their proposed business contributes to climate resilience or climate-smart agriculture.

This could involve demonstrating how the project responds to environmental challenges or promotes more sustainable agricultural practices.

Applicants should clearly explain the connection between their business model and climate resilience.

Explain the Revenue Model

Entrepreneurs must explain how their business intends to generate income.

A strong revenue model should clearly demonstrate how the venture can become financially sustainable.

Applicants may need to consider questions such as:

  • Who will pay for the product or service?
  • What will customers purchase?
  • How will the business generate revenue?
  • How frequently will revenue be generated?
  • What are the main sources of income?
  • What makes the business financially viable?

A clear revenue model is important because it demonstrates that the project is not simply an idea but has the potential to operate as a sustainable enterprise.

Estimate the Capital Required

Applicants must provide an estimate of the financial resources needed to start or scale the proposed project.

This should include a realistic assessment of the capital required for implementation.

Potential costs may include:

  • Equipment
  • Raw materials
  • Technology
  • Production
  • Marketing
  • Transportation
  • Staffing
  • Facilities
  • Licensing
  • Business development

Applicants should make reasonable and well-considered estimates based on the nature and scale of their proposed venture.

Can Applicants Save Their Submission and Return Later?

Yes.

The KoboToolbox submission form allows applicants to save a draft and return later.

This feature gives entrepreneurs the opportunity to take their time when developing their responses.

Applicants should use this flexibility to carefully review their AgriCanvas, climate-smart strategy, revenue model and capital requirements before submitting the final application.

However, saving a draft should not be confused with submitting the application.

Applicants must ensure that the final submission is completed before the deadline.

Can You Submit More Than One Business Idea?

No.

Each applicant may submit only one idea per submission window.

Applicants should therefore carefully select the strongest and most viable business concept before completing their application.

The organisers have also indicated that where multiple submissions are made using the same course certificate ID, only the last complete and valid submission will be considered.

Any additional submissions using the same certificate ID may be disregarded.

This makes it particularly important for applicants to review their proposal carefully before submitting it.

What Happens If You Are Not Selected?

Applicants who are not selected during the current submission window are encouraged not to give up.

Entrepreneurship often involves refining and improving ideas over time.

Unsuccessful applicants may have the opportunity to:

  • Improve their business concept
  • Strengthen their AgriCanvas
  • Continue learning through e-MOVE
  • Improve their financial projections
  • Develop a stronger climate-smart component
  • Refine their revenue model
  • Resubmit their idea in a future submission window

The organisers indicate that unsuccessful applicants will not necessarily receive individual notifications.

However, important announcements and future submission opportunities are expected to be shared through official channels.

When Will Successful Applicants Be Notified?

Successful applicants are expected to be contacted by mid-December 2026.

Applicants should ensure that they provide accurate contact information when completing their submission.

They should also monitor their email and official programme communication channels after submitting their proposal.

How Will Winners Be Selected?

The evaluation process and selection criteria are outlined in the official Terms and Conditions document.

Applicants are encouraged to review the Terms and Conditions carefully before submitting their proposals.

Understanding the evaluation criteria can help entrepreneurs prepare stronger applications and ensure that their submissions align with the expectations of the programme.

A competitive proposal should generally demonstrate:

  • Innovation
  • Practicality
  • Business viability
  • Investment potential
  • Clear revenue generation
  • Climate-smart practices
  • Resilience
  • Relevance to the value chain
  • Realistic capital requirements
  • Potential for growth and impact

Applicants should focus on clearly communicating why their idea matters and how it can realistically be implemented.

What Value Chains Are Eligible?

For the e-MOVE Call for Proposals, applicants should focus on the cashew value chain.

The broader programme information also references opportunities connected to other value chains under the Agribusiness e-Academy, including:

  • Maize
  • Livestock, including cattle, sheep and goats
  • Cocoa

However, applicants should carefully follow the requirements of the specific submission window and programme pathway they are applying under.

Ideas submitted outside the eligible value chains may not be considered.

For this particular e-MOVE opportunity, applicants should ensure that their proposal clearly demonstrates a connection to the cashew sector.

Who Is Organising the Competition?

The competition is organised by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH through initiatives including:

  • The Agri-Business Facility for Africa (ABF)
  • Market-Oriented Value Chains for Jobs and Growth in the ECOWAS Region (MOVE-ComCashew)

Both initiatives are part of German Development Cooperation.

The projects contribute to the Joint Action:

Business Support Facility for Resilient Agricultural Value Chains

The Joint Action brings together several development partners and institutions, including:

  • The European Union Directorate-General for International Partnerships (INTPA)
  • The Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States (OACPS)
  • The German Government
  • The Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ)

The initiative is jointly co-financed by the European Union under the Samoa Agreement with OACPS and by BMZ, with implementation support provided by GIZ.

Important Things to Remember Before Applying

Before submitting an application, candidates should carefully check that they have completed all requirements.

Here is a useful application checklist:

Eligibility Checklist

  • You are at least 18 years old
  • You are based in an eligible OACPS member state
  • You have an innovative idea connected to the cashew value chain
  • You are interested in developing a climate-smart agribusiness venture

Training Checklist

  • You have registered on the e-MOVE or atingi platform
  • You have completed Introduction to Conservation Agriculture
  • You have completed Creating an Investment-Ready Agribusiness
  • You have obtained a valid certificate ID from the required final course

Submission Checklist

  • You have developed a complete AgriCanvas
  • Your idea focuses on the eligible cashew value chain
  • You have explained the climate-smart or resilience component
  • You have developed a clear revenue model
  • You have estimated your capital requirements
  • You have entered your AgriCanvas directly into the official form
  • You have reviewed all responses before submitting
  • You have submitted before the deadline

Tips for Preparing a Strong AgriCanvas Submission

Applicants should approach the competition as an opportunity to develop a real business concept rather than simply filling out an application form.

Here are several tips that may help strengthen a proposal.

1. Identify a Real Problem

Strong business ideas often begin with a clearly identified problem.

Think about challenges within the cashew value chain that affect:

  • Farmers
  • Processors
  • Traders
  • Consumers
  • Exporters
  • Rural communities

Your proposed solution should demonstrate how it addresses a specific need.

2. Be Specific About Your Customers

Clearly identify who will benefit from or purchase your product or service.

Avoid describing your target market too broadly.

Instead, consider specific customer groups and their needs.

3. Develop a Realistic Revenue Model

Explain exactly how the business will generate income.

An innovative idea is important, but a sustainable business must also have a clear path toward financial viability.

4. Integrate Climate-Smart Solutions

Think carefully about how your project can contribute to environmental sustainability and resilience.

Do not treat the climate-smart component as an afterthought.

Instead, integrate it directly into your business model.

5. Make Realistic Financial Estimates

Your capital requirements should be reasonable and connected to the actual needs of your proposed venture.

Avoid unrealistic figures or estimates that cannot be explained.

6. Demonstrate Innovation

Innovation does not necessarily mean inventing an entirely new product.

Innovation can involve improving an existing process, introducing new technology, developing a better business model or adapting a successful solution to a new market.

7. Review Your Application Before Submission

Before submitting, carefully check:

  • Spelling and grammar
  • Certificate information
  • Business model details
  • Revenue projections
  • Climate-smart components
  • Capital estimates
  • Completeness of responses

A well-organised and clearly written submission can make it easier for evaluators to understand your idea.

APPLY HERE

Deadline

The deadline for submitting proposals under Submission Window 3 is: 30 October 2026

Applicants are strongly encouraged to begin the required courses and develop their AgriCanvas early.

Since completion of the mandatory training is required before submitting an idea, waiting until the final days of the submission window may create unnecessary pressure.

Starting early gives applicants sufficient time to:

  1. Complete both mandatory courses.
  2. Understand the learning materials.
  3. Develop a strong business idea.
  4. Build a detailed AgriCanvas.
  5. Refine the revenue model.
  6. Identify climate-smart components.
  7. Estimate capital requirements.
  8. Review the final application.
  9. Submit before the deadline.

How to Apply

Interested and eligible applicants should begin by accessing the e-MOVE learning pathway, completing the mandatory courses and preparing their AgriCanvas.

Applicants can access the programme resources through the official platforms.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Call for Proposals 2026.

Conclusion

The e-MOVE Call for Proposals 2026: Build Your AgriCanvas. Build Your Future provides an important opportunity for young and emerging entrepreneurs to transform innovative cashew sector ideas into structured, investment-ready and climate-smart business ventures.

Beyond the possibility of receiving EUR 2,000 in direct funding or valuable business equipment, participants benefit from free agricultural and entrepreneurship training that can help them develop practical skills for building sustainable enterprises.

The programme is particularly valuable because it encourages applicants to think beyond an initial idea. Participants must consider how their businesses will generate revenue, respond to climate challenges, attract investment and contribute to resilient agricultural value chains.

For aspiring agripreneurs across eligible OACPS member states, this Call for Proposals presents an opportunity to combine learning, innovation and entrepreneurship while contributing to the future of the cashew industry.

Eligible applicants should begin the mandatory e-MOVE courses as early as possible, carefully develop their AgriCanvas and ensure their final submission is completed before the 30 October 2026 deadline.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the Airbus Global Graduate Programme 2027, offering an exciting opportunity for a recently graduated engineer to begin a career as a Satellite Assembly, Integration and Test (AIT) Electrical Engineer in Stevenage, United Kingdom.

The position is designed for graduates who want to work at the intersection of electrical engineering, spacecraft systems, software, testing and the space industry. Successful candidates will join Airbus Defence and Space and participate in a structured two-year graduate development journey beginning in September 2027.

Rather than simply offering an entry-level position, Airbus describes the programme as a development pathway intended to build technical expertise, business understanding, communication skills and future leadership capabilities. The successful graduate will receive practical exposure to spacecraft integration and testing while contributing to projects connected to major space missions.

About the Airbus Global Graduate Programme 2027

The Airbus Global Graduate Programme is designed to help recent university graduates transition from academic study into professional careers within one of the world’s leading aerospace organisations.

The programme combines practical employment with structured professional development. Graduates are expected to become productive members of their teams from the beginning while receiving support to strengthen their technical, interpersonal and leadership capabilities.

According to the vacancy, the two-year development journey includes areas such as:

  • Inclusive leadership
  • Airbus values
  • Resilience
  • Communication
  • Emotional intelligence
  • Business understanding
  • Technical development
  • Professional collaboration
  • Leadership preparation

Graduates will also become part of a global graduate community and participate in an annual in-person development week. This provides opportunities to meet fellow graduates, interact with experienced Airbus leaders and learn more about the wider organisation.

The programme is therefore particularly suitable for candidates looking for more than their first job and who want a structured route into a long-term aerospace career.

Graduate Satellite AIT Electrical Engineer Role

The successful candidate will follow a development pathway toward becoming a Satellite Assembly, Integration and Test Electrical Engineer.

Satellite AIT is a critical part of spacecraft development. Before a spacecraft can be launched, its systems and subsystems must be assembled, integrated, tested and verified to ensure they work correctly and meet the required technical specifications.

In this role, the graduate can expect to gain exposure to a broad range of spacecraft subsystems and learn how the Satellite Assembly Integration and Test department operates.

Airbus highlights experience with major European space missions, including:

  • Solar Orbiter
  • BIOMASS
  • ExoMars Rover

The organisation is also involved in projects relating to secure space communications for the UK Government.

This means the graduate could gain exposure to highly specialised work involving spacecraft technologies, testing processes and systems used in major space programmes.

What Will You Do?

The role provides exposure to both electrical engineering and software-related activities, making it particularly interesting for graduates who have interdisciplinary interests.

Responsibilities and development activities may include:

1. Spacecraft subsystem integration

The graduate will learn how different spacecraft subsystems are integrated into a functioning spacecraft.

This involves understanding how individual systems interact and ensuring that the interfaces between components operate as intended.

2. Functional and system testing

Testing is a major part of the position. The graduate will develop knowledge of spacecraft functional and system-level testing.

This may involve:

  • Conducting electrical measurements
  • Running test procedures
  • Analysing test results
  • Identifying unexpected behaviour
  • Supporting troubleshooting activities
  • Documenting test outcomes

3. Anomaly investigation

Spacecraft testing can reveal unexpected results or technical anomalies. The graduate will develop skills in investigating these issues and determining their possible causes.

This requires analytical thinking, attention to detail and the ability to make evidence-based decisions.

4. Programming and scripting

The role also offers opportunities to strengthen software and automation skills.

Airbus specifically mentions the use of:

  • C-based programming languages
  • Java
  • Bash scripting
  • Other scripting tools

Candidates with programming experience or a strong interest in developing their programming capabilities may therefore find this role particularly relevant.

5. Test documentation and reporting

Accurate documentation is essential in aerospace engineering.

The successful candidate will be expected to learn how to:

  • Record test results
  • Prepare technical documentation
  • Produce clear reports
  • Communicate technical information
  • Prepare presentations
  • Maintain accurate records of engineering activities

6. Environmental testing

The graduate may support environmental test campaigns designed to assess spacecraft performance under conditions relevant to launch and operation.

This can provide valuable experience in understanding how spacecraft systems are verified before deployment.

7. Launch-site activities

The role may also involve supporting spacecraft interface checks at launch sites.

Because Airbus states that the organisation supports spacecraft launches and environmental test campaigns, the position may involve overseas travel.

This can provide graduates with international exposure and an opportunity to understand how spacecraft move from development and testing toward launch.

Rotational Placement

An important feature of the graduate programme is the opportunity to undertake at least one rotational placement.

The rotation is intended to broaden the graduate’s experience and support development toward the eventual Satellite AIT Electrical Engineer position.

This can help the successful candidate understand different aspects of Airbus’ operations while developing a broader professional perspective.

Skills and Qualifications Required

Applicants should have a degree or equivalent qualification in a relevant engineering discipline.

Airbus identifies the following academic backgrounds as suitable:

  • Electronics Engineering
  • Electrical Systems Engineering
  • Avionics Engineering
  • Space Engineering
  • Similar engineering disciplines

Applicants should also be recent graduates or have first professional experience in engineering.

In addition to academic qualifications, Airbus is looking for candidates who demonstrate strong communication, teamwork and personal-development capabilities.

Technical Skills and Experience

Candidates are expected to demonstrate an interest or experience in practical engineering applications.

The vacancy highlights several areas that may strengthen an application.

Engineering knowledge

Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in applying engineering knowledge practically rather than relying exclusively on theoretical understanding.

Programming and scripting

Knowledge of programming and scripting is desirable, particularly experience with technologies such as:

  • C
  • Java
  • Bash scripting
  • Other programming or scripting languages

Candidates should be prepared to explain how they have applied these skills through university projects, personal projects, internships, employment or other technical activities.

Problem-solving

The position requires graduates who enjoy identifying solutions to technically complex problems.

Applicants should demonstrate an ability to:

  • Analyse problems logically
  • Investigate anomalies
  • Evaluate evidence
  • Develop practical solutions
  • Make informed decisions

Communication

Strong written and verbal communication skills are important because the engineer will need to work with technical teams and communicate engineering information clearly.

Applicants should be able to:

  • Listen carefully
  • Understand technical information
  • Explain information clearly
  • Prepare accurate documentation
  • Communicate effectively with colleagues

Teamwork

Airbus is looking for graduates who can work collaboratively in a technical environment.

A positive, proactive and reliable approach is important, particularly because spacecraft development involves multidisciplinary teams working toward common objectives.

Personal Qualities Airbus Is Looking For

Beyond technical qualifications, successful candidates should demonstrate several professional qualities.

These include:

  • A proactive, “can-do” attitude
  • Reliability
  • Teamwork
  • Self-awareness
  • Curiosity
  • Creativity
  • Strong communication
  • Willingness to learn
  • Interest in technical problem-solving
  • Evidence-based decision-making
  • Desire for continuous development
  • Ability to work in an open and trusting environment

Airbus also places emphasis on candidates taking responsibility for their own development.

Therefore, applicants should demonstrate not only what they already know but also how they intend to continue learning and improving.

Why This Graduate Opportunity Is Significant

The Airbus Global Graduate Programme provides several advantages for someone starting a career in aerospace.

Structured professional development

Instead of being left to navigate an entry-level position independently, graduates receive a structured two-year development programme.

Aerospace industry experience

The role provides an opportunity to work directly with spacecraft-related engineering activities.

Exposure to major space programmes

The vacancy references missions including Solar Orbiter, BIOMASS and ExoMars Rover, providing an indication of the scale and technical significance of projects associated with the organisation.

Technical and software development

The position combines electrical engineering with software and scripting, allowing graduates to develop interdisciplinary capabilities.

International exposure

The role may involve overseas travel in connection with environmental testing and spacecraft launches.

Leadership development

The programme includes training intended to develop future leadership capabilities.

Global graduate network

Participants will join a global graduate community and have opportunities to interact with graduates and experienced Airbus leaders.

Potential long-term career development

At the conclusion of the two-year programme, the graduate is expected to have developed into the position of Satellite AIT Electrical Engineer.

This makes the programme particularly attractive to candidates who want to build a long-term career in aerospace rather than simply obtain short-term graduate employment.

Recruitment and Selection Process

Airbus outlines a multi-stage recruitment process for the opportunity.

The process is expected to follow these stages:

  1. Online application
  2. Online task-based assessment
  3. Application review
  4. Virtual assessment centre
  5. Offer

The application will initially be reviewed by the Talent Acquisition Partner and hiring manager.

Candidates who progress through the process should therefore be prepared to demonstrate both their technical capabilities and their suitability for Airbus’ working environment.

Application Deadline

The official application deadline is:

30 September 2026

However, applicants are strongly encouraged to submit their applications early.

Airbus specifically warns that some roles may close before the stated deadline if a sufficient number of applications are received.

Applicants should therefore avoid waiting until the final day.

Important Visa and Work-Eligibility Information

One of the most important considerations for international applicants is the position’s work-authorisation requirement.

Airbus states that it cannot provide Skilled Worker visa sponsorship for this position.

The company welcomes applications from candidates who already have the right to work in the United Kingdom or who qualify to work through other available routes, such as the:

  • Graduate Visa
  • Youth Mobility Scheme
  • Other eligible immigration routes

Applicants should independently verify their eligibility under current UK immigration requirements before applying.

For detailed and official immigration information, candidates should consult UK Visas and Immigration.

Application Documents

Applications and CVs must be submitted in English.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their CV clearly presents:

  • Their relevant engineering degree
  • Technical skills
  • Programming experience
  • Engineering projects
  • Practical experience
  • Relevant internships or work experience
  • Teamwork experience
  • Problem-solving abilities
  • Communication skills
  • Academic or personal projects relevant to aerospace or engineering

Where possible, candidates should demonstrate achievements rather than simply listing skills.

For example, instead of stating that they have “programming skills,” an applicant could describe a university or personal project where they used C, Java, Bash or another language to solve a specific engineering problem.

How to Strengthen Your Application

Because Airbus asks applicants to submit only one application to the Airbus Global Graduate Programme, candidates should carefully select the opportunity that best matches their background.

Before submitting your application, consider the following:

1. Tailor your CV

Make the most relevant engineering, programming and practical experience easy for the recruiter to identify.

2. Highlight practical projects

University projects, engineering laboratories, programming projects, robotics projects, electronics projects and other hands-on experiences can help demonstrate practical ability.

3. Demonstrate problem-solving

Use examples that show how you identified a problem, analysed it and developed a solution.

4. Explain your interest in aerospace

A strong application should make it clear why you want to work in aerospace and why spacecraft AIT interests you.

5. Show interdisciplinary skills

Because the role combines electrical engineering, spacecraft systems and software, applicants should highlight experience across multiple technical areas where applicable.

6. Demonstrate teamwork

Spacecraft development is highly collaborative. Include examples showing your ability to work effectively with others.

7. Prepare for the assessment

Since the recruitment process includes an online task-based assessment and virtual assessment centre, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate analytical thinking, communication and problem-solving skills.

8. Submit early

Although the deadline is 30 September 2026, some positions may close earlier because of application volume.

Accessibility and Inclusion

Airbus states that applicants can request adjustments during the recruitment process.

Examples may include:

  • Accessible facilities
  • Additional time for written exercises
  • Other reasonable adjustments

Candidates who require an adjustment are encouraged to communicate their needs to Airbus. The company states that information disclosed for this purpose will be treated confidentially.

Airbus also states its commitment to workforce diversity and an inclusive working environment and welcomes applications irrespective of factors including social and cultural background, age, gender, disability, sexual orientation or religious belief.

Who Can Apply?

Category of people who qualify

This opportunity is primarily intended for:

  • Recent university graduates
  • Early-career engineering professionals
  • Candidates with a degree or equivalent qualification in Electronics, Electrical Systems, Avionics, Space Engineering or a closely related engineering discipline
  • Candidates with an interest in spacecraft systems, electrical engineering, software, testing and aerospace
  • Candidates with strong English communication skills
  • Candidates who can demonstrate teamwork, problem-solving and practical engineering abilities
  • Candidates who are legally entitled to work in the UK through an existing or eligible route

Nationality and geographic eligibility

Airbus describes its Global Graduate Programme as seeking talented graduates from around the globe. However, this specific Satellite AIT Electrical Engineer position is based in Stevenage, United Kingdom, and Airbus states that Skilled Worker visa sponsorship is not available.

Therefore, international applicants should not assume that being eligible to apply automatically means they are eligible to work in the UK. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania and other regions may consider the opportunity if they independently meet the position’s work-authorisation requirements.

The key issue for candidates outside the UK is therefore existing or otherwise eligible UK work rights, rather than nationality alone.

Application Link

Interested candidates should review the complete vacancy requirements and submit their application through the official Airbus careers platform.

Application deadline: 30 September 2026

Candidates can also review Airbus’ recruitment guidance and application tips through Airbus Careers Recruitment Process & Tips.

APPLY HERE

About Airbus

Airbus is a major aerospace company operating across commercial aircraft, defence and security, helicopters and space.

The organisation describes its purpose around pioneering sustainable aerospace for a safe and united world. Its activities span technologically advanced aircraft, defence and security systems, connected services and space programmes.

For graduates interested in aerospace engineering, working at Airbus can provide exposure to complex international projects and multidisciplinary engineering environments.

Visit HERE to learn more about Airbus Global Graduate Programme 2027.

Final Thoughts

The Airbus Global Graduate Programme 2027 – Graduate Satellite AIT Electrical Engineer position represents a strong opportunity for recent engineering graduates who want to establish themselves in the aerospace and space sector.

The two-year programme combines employment with structured technical and professional development, giving graduates the opportunity to gain practical experience in spacecraft assembly, integration and testing while strengthening their electrical engineering, programming, problem-solving and communication capabilities.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to graduates with backgrounds in electronics, electrical systems, avionics, space engineering or related disciplines, especially those who have practical engineering experience and an interest in programming and spacecraft technology.

However, applicants should pay close attention to the UK work-authorisation requirement, as Airbus has explicitly stated that Skilled Worker visa sponsorship is not available for this position.

With applications closing on 30 September 2026, eligible candidates should prepare their English-language CV carefully, tailor their application to the role and submit well before the deadline, as Airbus notes that individual opportunities may close earlier if application numbers are high.

item.content:encoded:
NASA has released the final Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute Cooperative Agreement Notice-5 (SSERVI CAN-5), inviting multi-institutional research teams to compete for major cooperative agreement awards supporting lunar science, planetary exploration, NASA’s Artemis programme and research that uses the Moon to prepare for future exploration of Mars.

The final opportunity is:

SSERVI CAN-5 – NNH26ZDA016C

NASA’s Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate are jointly supporting the initiative. The call seeks integrated, multi-institutional teams capable of advancing fundamental and applied research on the Moon and its near-space environment, while strengthening connections between planetary science and human exploration. “Mars forward” projects that use lunar research to develop approaches relevant to eventual Mars exploration are explicitly welcomed.

The funding opportunity is particularly notable because teams can combine major scientific research with activities designed to strengthen the future STEM workforce and broaden public participation in NASA science.

The detailed CAN funding structure anticipates:

  • Approximately five awards
  • Up to approximately $1.8 million per year per team
  • An anticipated five-year award period
  • Approximately $9 million total per selected team over five years
  • Up to an average of $180,000 per year within the overall team budget for Workforce Development and/or Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps activities

The $180,000 is important to understand correctly: it is not an additional $180,000 on top of the $1.8 million annual award. It is part of the overall annual team budget and can support the additional workforce and engagement components.

The proposal process has two stages:

Step-1 Proposal Deadline: September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM Eastern Daylight Time

Step-2 Full Proposal Deadline: December 4, 2026

Only teams that submit the required Step-1 proposal may proceed to Step 2. NASA will use dual-anonymous peer review, and applicants must submit their proposals through NASA’s NSPIRES system rather than through Grants.gov.

Important update about the earlier draft

The document initially circulated for community comment was DRAFT SSERVI CAN-5, NNH26ZDA013J. That draft was issued on July 10, 2026 and closed for comments on July 28. NASA has since issued the final call as NNH26ZDA016C, so applicants should use the final announcement number and final deadlines rather than the dates or placeholders contained in the draft.

This article therefore uses NASA’s final announcement for the current solicitation number and deadlines, while drawing on the detailed CAN documentation supplied with the opportunity for the programme’s research structure, funding architecture and proposal requirements.

About NASA’s Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute

The Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute, or SSERVI, is a distributed research institute that brings together expertise from the scientific and human exploration communities.

Its premise is that:

Science enables exploration, and exploration enables science.

SSERVI is designed to create collaborative research teams rather than fund a collection of isolated individual projects.

The Institute connects researchers working across areas such as:

  • Lunar science
  • Planetary science
  • Space physics
  • Human exploration
  • Geology and geophysics
  • Engineering
  • Biological and physical sciences
  • Robotics
  • Sample science
  • Space environments
  • Technology
  • Public engagement
  • Workforce development

Selected teams become participating members of the broader SSERVI network and are expected to collaborate both internally and across other Institute teams.

The Institute is coordinated through SSERVI Central at NASA Ames Research Center. Its virtual structure enables geographically distributed universities, research organisations, NASA institutions, industry partners and other eligible organisations to work together on large interdisciplinary problems.

What NASA Is Looking for Through SSERVI CAN-5

NASA is not seeking disconnected small projects under this call.

It wants:

Multi-institutional, team-based, integrated research programmes.

The final announcement specifies that proposals should present innovative basic and/or applied research that advances understanding of:

  • The Moon
  • The Moon’s near-space environment
  • Scientific questions relevant to human lunar exploration
  • Research required to enable Artemis
  • Lunar research that can inform future Mars exploration

NASA says proposals complementing current CAN-4 SSERVI teams, or filling important research gaps not already covered by the Institute, will receive strong consideration.

Supporting NASA’s Artemis Programme

A central objective of CAN-5 is supporting NASA’s return to the Moon through:

  • Human missions
  • Robotic missions
  • Lunar surface research
  • Sample science
  • Exploration science
  • Development of scientific approaches supporting longer-duration lunar activity

The Moon is therefore not treated solely as a scientific destination.

It is also regarded as a location where researchers can develop knowledge, methods and operational experience necessary for future human exploration.

The “Mars Forward” Approach

NASA explicitly welcomes:

Mars-forward research

This means proposals may use studies of the Moon to develop:

  • Methods
  • Scientific knowledge
  • Operational approaches
  • Exploration concepts
  • Technologies

that could later inform Mars missions.

The Moon can serve as an intermediate environment for studying issues such as:

  • Long-duration surface operations
  • Radiation
  • Dust
  • Resource utilisation
  • Habitat sustainability
  • Robotics
  • Autonomous operations
  • Human-machine interaction
  • Sample handling

NASA’s final announcement specifically confirms that proposals using lunar-focused research to develop approaches to Mars exploration are welcome.

Anticipated Funding: Up to $1.8 Million Per Year

The detailed CAN funding table anticipates:

$9 million in first-year funding for all new awards

with approximately:

Five awards

at an anticipated level of:

$1.8 million per year for five years

or approximately:

$9 million per selected team over five years.

If five awards were funded at the anticipated maximum annual level across the full five-year period, the overall multi-year programme value could be substantial.

However, applicants should not interpret future-year funding as automatically guaranteed.

The detailed CAN notes that awards are generally not fully funded upfront and future-year funding depends on:

  • Congressional appropriations
  • Availability of NASA funding
  • Continued programme funding
  • Acceptable performance and award conditions

Applicants should therefore construct realistic five-year budgets while recognising the federal appropriations condition attached to out-year funding.

Up to $180,000 Per Year for Workforce Development, Citizen Science and Public Engagement

One of the most interesting features of SSERVI CAN-5 is its explicit integration of scientific research with wider workforce and community engagement.

The detailed CAN allows teams to request up to an average of:

$180,000 per year

across the proposed five-year period for the combined activities associated with:

  • Workforce Development Plan
  • Citizen Science Plan
  • Science Activation Plan
  • Space Apps Plan

Again, this amount is part of the overall SSERVI team budget rather than an additional award outside the main funding ceiling.

This provision creates an unusual opportunity for institutions that want to combine advanced lunar and planetary research with:

  • Student development
  • Postdoctoral training
  • STEM workforce development
  • Public participation in science
  • Science communication
  • Community engagement
  • Citizen science
  • NASA Space Apps activities

Workforce Development Plan

NASA places significant emphasis on preparing the next generation of researchers, scientists and engineers.

The Workforce Development Plan should describe how the team will:

  • Build knowledge
  • Develop technical or professional skills
  • Promote collaboration
  • Support professional growth
  • Prepare students and early-career researchers
  • Address changing workforce needs

The detailed CAN identifies possible activities such as:

  • Specialized undergraduate courses
  • Graduate courses
  • Workshops
  • Postdoctoral training opportunities
  • Field training
  • Internships
  • New degree programmes
  • Collaborative training initiatives

NASA also encourages partnerships that expand access to relevant knowledge and skills.

What the Workforce Development Plan Must Explain

The plan should clearly identify:

  • Objectives
  • Proposed activities
  • Approach
  • Expected outcomes
  • Potential impact
  • How the programme contributes to training future planetary scientists and engineers
  • How progress will be evaluated

An evaluation approach is required so the team can assess progress against its stated workforce objectives and identify areas for improvement.

Citizen Science Opportunities

SSERVI teams must also connect their activities with NASA’s broader public-engagement ecosystem.

The detailed solicitation allows proposals to include a:

Citizen Science Plan

A team may either:

  • Establish a new citizen-science project
  • Collaborate with an existing NASA-supported citizen-science project
  • Combine both approaches

Citizen science involves members of the public actively contributing to scientific research.

NASA expects these projects to maintain rigorous scientific standards and involve meaningful interaction between professional scientists and volunteers.

What a New Citizen Science Project Should Address

Teams proposing a new citizen-science initiative should explain issues including:

  • The relevant scientific field
  • Scientific questions being investigated
  • Citizen-science methodology
  • How the public contribution helps answer the research question
  • Why citizen science is an appropriate method
  • Relevant existing communities or platforms
  • Beta testing where necessary
  • Team expertise
  • How participants will be informed about project outcomes

The programme therefore treats citizen science as a genuine research method rather than simply a promotional activity.

Science Activation Plan

Teams can alternatively or additionally develop a:

Science Activation Plan

NASA’s Science Activation, or SciAct, approach aims to connect people of different ages and backgrounds with NASA science.

Activities might include:

  • Learning experiences
  • Workshops
  • Webinars
  • Educational resources
  • Training
  • Engagement with NASA subject-matter experts
  • Public events
  • Science experiences

The objective is to connect SSERVI-generated knowledge with established NASA Science Activation audiences and dissemination networks.

Space Apps Plan

Teams may also develop a:

Space Apps Plan

NASA’s International Space Apps Challenge is a global hackathon encouraging participants to use NASA data and resources to address challenges related to Earth and space.

A SSERVI team proposing a Space Apps component should consider developing relevant challenges and engaging subject-matter experts capable of supporting participants.

The detailed CAN indicates that Space Apps plans should explain:

  • The challenge idea
  • The problem participants will address
  • Desired outcomes
  • Relevant experts and support

A Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps Plan Is Expected

The detailed CAN states that SSERVI proposals should contain an engagement plan involving:

  • Citizen Science,
  • Science Activation,
  • Space Apps,

or some combination of these approaches.

Teams should identify a relevant liaison, subject-matter experts, personnel and corresponding budget.

This means public engagement is not simply an optional paragraph added at the end of the science proposal.

It is integrated into how NASA expects SSERVI teams to contribute to the wider scientific ecosystem.

Major Scientific Research Areas

The CAN supports a broad range of lunar and exploration research.

The detailed research list is explicitly non-exhaustive, meaning teams do not have to cover every area.

Potential research areas include the following.

Fundamental Lunar Geology

Research may examine:

  • Origin of the Moon
  • Internal structure
  • Mass anomalies
  • Core structure and formation
  • Surface evolution
  • Volcanic history
  • Tectonic history
  • Thermal evolution
  • Planetary differentiation
  • Lunar magma ocean
  • Crater distributions
  • Impact history
  • Earth-Moon system evolution

Lunar Environment

Research may examine the environmental conditions surrounding and affecting the Moon.

Possible subjects include:

  • Solar wind
  • Space weathering
  • Lunar exosphere
  • Plasma processes
  • Magnetic fields
  • Radiation environment
  • Effects of deep-space radiation
  • Effects of lunar albedo radiation on biological systems

Lunar Volatiles

The distribution and behaviour of volatiles are important both scientifically and for future exploration.

Potential research includes:

  • Origin of lunar volatiles
  • Chemical composition
  • Distribution
  • Transport
  • Sequestration
  • Regolith interactions
  • Volatiles in lunar samples
  • Permanently shadowed regions
  • Temperatures and lighting conditions
  • Depth and distribution of resources

Lunar Regolith

Regolith research is particularly relevant to future human and robotic surface activity.

Possible subjects include:

  • Formation and evolution
  • Particle size distribution
  • Geotechnical properties
  • Geochemistry
  • High-fidelity simulants
  • Robot-regolith interactions
  • Plume-surface interactions
  • Material extraction
  • Gas extraction
  • Partial-gravity effects
  • Regolith interactions with crop plants

Lunar Dust

Dust can affect:

  • Human health
  • Robotic equipment
  • Mechanical systems
  • Surface operations
  • Scientific instruments

Relevant research could examine:

  • Dust composition
  • Dust mobility
  • Particle size
  • Charge
  • Adhesion
  • Cohesion
  • Plasma-driven transport
  • Mechanical effects on systems

Returned Samples and Meteorites

SSERVI research can also include investigations involving:

  • Petrology
  • Geochemistry
  • Mineralogy
  • Geophysical properties
  • Magnetic properties
  • Geotechnical properties

of returned lunar samples and meteorites.

Sample Management

Relevant research may address:

  • Sample preservation
  • Storage
  • Collection
  • Return protocols
  • New analytical methods

Sample science is particularly significant as NASA prepares for future Artemis surface activities and potential sample return.

Cosmic Rays and Solar Storms

Proposals may study galactic cosmic rays and solar events in relation to:

  • Crew risk
  • Hardware risk
  • Mitigation approaches

Understanding the radiation environment is essential for longer-duration human activity beyond Earth.

Robotics, Automation and Autonomous Systems

Relevant areas may include:

  • Robotics
  • Sample handling
  • Automated analysis
  • Automated operations
  • Telerobotics
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Machine learning
  • Autonomous systems
  • Augmented reality
  • Virtual reality

The detailed CAN indicates that new technological approaches are welcome where they form part of a broader integrated scientific programme.

Planetary Protection

Possible areas include:

  • Survival of terrestrial organisms in extraterrestrial environments
  • Radiation exposure
  • Vacuum
  • Extreme temperatures
  • Microbial management
  • Antimicrobial approaches
  • Waste management
  • Prevention of microbial growth and spread

The Moon as a Scientific Platform

The unique lunar environment may also support research into broader astrophysical and fundamental-physics questions.

Examples listed in the CAN include:

  • Low-frequency radio astronomy
  • Dark Ages cosmology
  • Gravitational-wave concepts
  • Tests of general relativity
  • Cosmic-ray astrophysics
  • Observations uniquely enabled by the lunar environment

The programme therefore extends beyond conventional lunar geology.

Multi-Institutional Collaboration Is Required

A defining feature of the SSERVI model is collaboration.

Teams must involve expertise from:

More than one institution.

The programme also expects varied technical expertise rather than a team composed exclusively of researchers working in a single narrow subfield.

Research tasks should be intellectually connected.

A proposal that divides funding among unrelated projects without a convincing unifying research structure is unlikely to reflect the Institute model.

Who Can Apply?

This is primarily an institutional research funding opportunity, not an individual scholarship or personal fellowship.

Eligible entities identified in the detailed CAN include several categories.

Educational Organisations

Potentially eligible institutions include:

  • Public institutions of higher education
  • State-controlled universities
  • Private institutions of higher education
  • Independent school districts

Nonprofit Organisations

The detailed CAN lists:

  • 501(c)(3) nonprofit organisations
  • Eligible nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status

Government Organisations

Categories include:

  • State governments
  • County governments
  • City or township governments
  • Special district governments
  • Tribal governments

For-Profit Organisations

Eligible categories include:

  • For-profit organisations
  • Small businesses meeting relevant SBA size requirements

The detailed programme description also identifies research organisations such as universities, industry partners, FFRDCs, NASA Centers and other U.S. government agencies as part of the target research community.

Lead Institution Requirement

For multi-organisational proposals, one organisation serves as the:

Lead Institution

The detailed CAN states that this should be the:

Principal Investigator’s home institution.

NASA funding is provided to U.S. institutions under the solicitation framework.

The final public opportunity listing likewise states that proposers must be affiliated with institutions registered in NSPIRES and that NASA generally provides funding only to U.S. institutions.

Can International Researchers Participate?

Yes, but with an important distinction.

The opportunity is not structured as an internationally funded grant where institutions worldwide can independently lead and receive NASA funding.

Instead:

NASA generally provides funding to U.S. institutions.

International researchers and institutions may participate through collaborations conducted under NASA’s applicable no-exchange-of-funds rules.

The detailed CAN encourages U.S. proposers to collaborate with international researchers, including relevant existing SSERVI international partners and other appropriate organisations, while making clear that international lead institutions are not solicited.

Restriction Concerning China and Chinese-Owned Companies

The detailed CAN contains a specific institutional and national-participation restriction.

It states that proposals involving bilateral participation, collaboration or coordination with China or Chinese-owned companies, whether funded or under a no-exchange-of-funds arrangement, are ineligible for award under the solicitation.

Applicants involved in international partnerships should therefore read the final CAN and NASA Grants and Cooperative Agreements Manual carefully before building the proposal team.

Is Cost Sharing Required?

No.

The detailed CAN states:

Cost sharing is not required.

NASA may accept voluntary cost sharing, but it is not a prerequisite for competing for the award.

Two-Step Application Process

SSERVI CAN-5 uses a mandatory two-stage proposal process.

This is one of the most important requirements to understand.

Step 1: Preliminary Proposal

Step-1 proposals are due:

September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM EDT.

Submitting Step 1 is mandatory.

NASA’s final announcement confirms:

Only proposers that submit Step 1 are eligible to submit Step 2.

What Goes Into Step 1?

The detailed CAN describes Step 1 as a short preliminary summary.

The core submission uses the NSPIRES:

4,000-character Proposal Summary field.

No full budget is required at this stage.

NASA requests information including:

  • Principal Investigator
  • Institution
  • Contact details
  • Co-Investigators and known team members
  • Proposed project title
  • Brief investigation description

The Step-1 proposal must be submitted by the organisation’s Authorized Organizational Representative, or AOR.

Teams therefore need to involve their institution’s research administration office early.

Register Early in NSPIRES and SAM

Organisations and participating investigators need to be registered in:

NASA NSPIRES

NASA also notes that organisations must have valid System for Award Management (SAM) registration before registering in NSPIRES.

The detailed CAN warns that SAM registration can take significant time.

This makes early institutional coordination especially important.

Do not wait until September 29 to begin organizational registration.

Team Members Must Confirm Participation

The detailed application instructions also require relevant team members to confirm participation through NSPIRES.

A proposal cannot be submitted if required team members have not completed their participation confirmation and organizational relationship requirements.

This is another reason Principal Investigators should build their team early.

Step 2: Full Proposal

Full proposals are due:

December 4, 2026.

The final call uses:

Dual-Anonymous Peer Review

or:

DAPR

for proposal evaluation.

Step 2 is split into:

  • Volume A – Anonymous material
  • Volume B – Non-anonymous material

Anonymous Volume A

The detailed CAN identifies major components of Volume A including:

  • Proposal Cover Page
  • Table of Contents
  • Executive Summary
  • Research Plan
  • Anonymized Personnel and Work Effort Table
  • Redacted Budget and Narrative
  • Open Science and Data Management Plan
  • References
  • Workforce Development Plan
  • Fieldwork Plan, where applicable
  • Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps Plan

The draft specifies a substantial 35-page Research Plan, along with three-page limits for several specialized plans.

Applicants should consult the final CAN before submission for the definitive page and format limits.

Non-Anonymous Volume B

The detailed CAN describes the non-anonymous section as containing institutional and personnel information, including areas such as:

  • Team Collaboration and Science Management
  • Team agreements on acceptable behaviour
  • Fieldwork agreements where relevant
  • Contributions to SSERVI and NASA’s mission
  • Biographical sketches
  • Personnel and work-effort information
  • Current and pending support
  • Letters of commitment or support
  • Facilities and equipment information
  • High-End Computing information where required

NASA separates these materials from anonymous scientific content to protect the integrity of the dual-anonymous review.

Open Science and Data Management

SSERVI CAN-5 also places emphasis on:

  • Open science
  • Data management
  • Accessible research
  • Peer review
  • Responsible dissemination

Teams should therefore treat their data-management plan as a substantive component rather than an administrative afterthought.

Contribution to the Wider SSERVI Community

Selected teams are expected to contribute to the Institute beyond their own research programme.

Possible contributions may include:

  • Professional community development
  • Workshops
  • Seminar series
  • Cross-team collaboration
  • Research tools
  • Data visualisation
  • AI and machine-learning applications
  • Shared scientific facilities
  • Commercial space partnerships
  • International partnerships

The detailed CAN explicitly emphasizes that SSERVI is more than a collection of independent projects.

What NASA Will Evaluate

The final NASA announcement confirms that proposals will undergo peer review under the rules set out in the CAN.

Broad assessment considerations include:

  • Scientific and technical merit
  • Quality of the proposed research
  • Relevance to SSERVI
  • Relevance to NASA’s lunar and exploration priorities
  • Integration across disciplines
  • Open Science and Data Management
  • Workforce Development
  • Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps
  • Team collaboration and management
  • Cost reasonableness

The final call also gives strong consideration to proposals that either complement existing CAN-4 teams or address important gaps in the existing SSERVI research portfolio.

Application Timeline

The major confirmed dates for the final CAN-5 opportunity are:

Stage Date
Final CAN-5 available 2026
Step-1 proposal September 29, 2026, 11:59:59 PM EDT
Step-2 full proposal December 4, 2026
Anticipated award notification Approximately nine months after Step 2, according to the detailed CAN structure

NASA’s official final announcement confirms the September 29 and December 4 proposal deadlines.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through:

NASA NSPIRES

They cannot be submitted as applications directly through the Grants.gov synopsis.

Open the final SSERVI CAN-5 opportunity in NSPIRES

NASA’s current announcement number is:

NNH26ZDA016C

Applicants should use this number when searching NSPIRES.

For the NASA announcement explaining the final release:

Read NASA’s SSERVI CAN-5 final text announcement

Programme questions can be directed to:

HQ-SSERVI@mail.nasa.gov

NASA requests clarification questions sufficiently before the Step-2 deadline; the final announcement specifies that questions should be submitted no later than 14 calendar days before Step 2.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive SSERVI CAN-5 Proposal

1. Do Not Treat This as an Individual Research Grant

SSERVI wants a:

Multi-institutional team

with a coherent intellectual programme.

A collection of unrelated researchers and projects is unlikely to demonstrate the integration NASA is seeking.

2. Make the Artemis Connection Explicit

Explain exactly how the proposed science contributes to:

  • Understanding the Moon
  • Lunar exploration
  • Artemis
  • Future human exploration

Do not assume reviewers will make the connection themselves.

3. Explain the “Mars Forward” Value Where Relevant

If your research can help future Mars exploration, explain:

  • What lunar problem is being studied
  • What can be learned on the Moon
  • How that knowledge translates to Mars

A credible Moon-to-Mars logic can strengthen the proposal.

4. Build the Workforce Plan as a Real Programme

The workforce component can represent up to an average of $180,000 per year together with public-engagement activities.

Treat it as a serious programme with:

  • Objectives
  • Beneficiaries
  • Activities
  • Expected outcomes
  • Evaluation

rather than a generic promise to “train students.”

5. Think Beyond Traditional Outreach

CAN-5 creates opportunities to integrate serious research with:

  • Citizen science
  • Science Activation
  • Space Apps
  • Workforce development

Teams with strong science and thoughtful engagement structures can potentially create much broader impact than through conventional outreach alone.

6. Identify the Right Institutional Lead

Because funding is primarily directed through U.S. institutions, international research groups should identify an appropriate eligible U.S. lead partner early.

The lead structure needs to be determined before Step 1.

7. Register in SAM and NSPIRES Immediately

Administrative registration can derail an otherwise strong proposal.

Confirm that:

  • Lead organisation has SAM registration
  • Institution is registered in NSPIRES
  • PI is registered
  • Co-Investigators are registered
  • Team members establish required organizational relationships
  • Required participants confirm participation

well before September 29.

8. Protect Proposal Anonymity

NASA is using dual-anonymous peer review.

Applicants should therefore carefully remove identifying information from anonymous materials.

This includes more than simply deleting the PI’s name.

The detailed CAN cautions against revealing identity through:

  • Institution names
  • Logos
  • Self-identifying references
  • Named collaborations
  • Possessive descriptions of previous work
  • Pronouns revealing team-member identity

9. Review Existing SSERVI Teams

NASA says proposals complementing CAN-4 teams or filling gaps in existing research coverage will receive strong consideration.

Before designing the proposal, review what SSERVI already funds.

Ask:

  • What important scientific problem is missing?
  • How does the proposed work complement existing teams?
  • What new capability would this team add?
  • Why does the Institute need this team now?

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute Cooperative Agreement Notice-5

Abbreviation: SSERVI CAN-5

Final announcement number: NNH26ZDA016C

Agency: NASA

NASA directorates: Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate

Primary focus: Moon, lunar environment, Artemis and Mars-forward exploration research

Step-1 deadline: September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM EDT

Conclusion

The NASA SSERVI CAN-5 2026 funding opportunity represents a major opportunity for universities, research institutions, nonprofits, industry partners, government research organisations and other eligible U.S.-based institutions to build ambitious multi-institutional teams focused on the future of lunar and planetary exploration.

Under final solicitation NNH26ZDA016C, NASA is seeking research programmes that can advance fundamental and applied understanding of the Moon and its near-space environment while contributing directly to Artemis and future human exploration. Mars-forward research using lunar science to develop approaches relevant to Mars is also explicitly encouraged.

The detailed CAN funding structure anticipates approximately five awards at around $1.8 million per year for five years, equivalent to approximately $9 million per team over the proposed award period, subject to federal appropriations and continued funding.

A particularly distinctive element is the opportunity to dedicate up to an average of $180,000 per year within the overall budget to Workforce Development and Citizen Science, Science Activation and/or Space Apps activities.

This creates room for institutions to combine frontier research with serious investment in:

  • Students
  • Early-career researchers
  • Postdoctoral scholars
  • STEM workforce pathways
  • Public participation
  • Citizen science
  • Science communication
  • Community engagement

Applications use a mandatory two-stage process. Step-1 proposals are due September 29, 2026, and only Step-1 proposers can proceed to the December 4, 2026 Step-2 deadline.

For teams working in lunar science, planetary science, human exploration, workforce development or meaningful public participation in NASA science, SSERVI CAN-5 is one of the most significant NASA team-research opportunities currently open.
